cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: keeping utilization in the 40-60% range
cards.claim: Design the whole workflow around context management and keep context-window utilization at roughly 40-60%, depending on problem complexity.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as the working rule behind 'frequent intentional compaction'; no measurement of the band is given.
cards.landing: Phase routine: a context-use ceiling per phase; one phase per new session already approximates it

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: designing your ENTIRE WORKFLOW around context management
cards.claim: Frequent intentional compaction means the process itself (research, plan, implement) is shaped so each step ends in a compacted artifact and starts in a fresh window.
cards.evidence_detail: Claims of 300k LOC Rust work, 6 PRs in a day, a week of work in a day; no controlled comparison.
cards.landing: Ship plan §0 phase routine (one phase per new chat, decisions journal as the compaction artifact)

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Write everything we did so far to progress.md
cards.claim: Intentional compaction: when context fills, have the agent write goal, approach, steps done and current failure to a file, then start a fresh window.
cards.evidence_detail: Given as an example prompt; no results.
cards.landing: Phase routine: draft-PR body and decisions journal; cold-resume trial (P1) tests exactly this

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: You can also use commit messages for intentional compaction.
cards.claim: Commit messages can serve as the compaction artifact that carries state into the next session.
cards.evidence_detail: One-line aside linking an X post; nothing else.
cards.landing: Commit/PR conventions; the 'Plan @ <sha>' PR body

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Searching for files / Understanding code flow / Applying edits / Test/build logs / Huge JSON blobs from tools
cards.claim: The main context consumers are file search, code-flow understanding, edits, test/build logs and large tool JSON, and compaction distils them into structured artifacts.
cards.evidence_detail: A listed taxonomy; no sizes given.
cards.landing: Output caps on test/build logs and tool output; which verifier outputs are summarised before returning

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the contents of your context window are the ONLY lever you have
cards.claim: Because each agent turn is a stateless function of its context, context contents are the only lever for output quality and are worth obsessing over.
cards.evidence_detail: Argued from the 12-factor-agents premise; no data.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md content policy (what is always loaded)

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Incorrect Information, Missing Information, Too much Noise
cards.claim: Rank the worst context failures as incorrect information first, missing information second, noise third; optimise for correctness, completeness, size, trajectory.
cards.evidence_detail: Ordered list with a joke equation; no measurement.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim criteria: stale or wrong prose is worse than long prose; knowledge-store verification

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: other
cards.quote: you only have approximately 170k of context window to work with.
cards.claim: Dex quotes Geoff Huntley that only about 170k tokens of context are usable and the more you use, the worse the outcomes; Dex does not dismiss the while-loop (Ralph) answer.
cards.evidence_detail: Quoted number from Huntley; Dex says he is 'not entirely sure that it is dumb'.
cards.landing: Context budget per phase; looping agents with simple prompt as an alternative to long sessions

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Subagents are about context control.
cards.claim: Subagents exist to keep the parent's window clean (fresh-window search and summarising), not to model roles or personas.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated with a demo video; no numbers.
cards.landing: fixflow-explorer Haiku locator agent; design rule for any new custom agent (context-control purpose, not role-play)

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Getting a subagent to return this is not trivial
cards.claim: A subagent's return should look like a good compaction (file paths, line refs, key findings), and prompting it to do so takes real effort.
cards.evidence_detail: Image-backed claim; no examples in text.
cards.landing: Output format spec in .claude/agents/fixflow-explorer.md

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The generic one works almost as well.
cards.claim: A generic Task() research prompt with a general-purpose subagent works almost as well as custom named subagents.
cards.evidence_detail: His own comparison across repos; no numbers.
cards.landing: Whether more custom agents are needed versus prompts/skills driving generic subagents

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: sometimes we skip the research and go straight to planning
cards.claim: Research/plan/implement is 'three-ish' steps: research may be skipped for simple work or repeated in several compacted passes before implementing.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes team practice.
cards.landing: Phase routine: which phases need a research step versus plan-only

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: being super precise about the testing / verification steps in each phase
cards.claim: A plan names exact files to edit and how, and states the test/verification step for each plan phase.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes the plan prompt; no results.
cards.landing: Plan template: per-phase verification step; reviewer fail-before/pass-after per register id

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I'll often compact the current status back into the original plan file
cards.claim: During implementation, write status back into the plan file after each verified phase so the plan doubles as the resume record.
cards.evidence_detail: Team practice for complex work.
cards.landing: Decisions journal / plan file status updates after each phase; cold-resume trial

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: this is the only step that needs to be done in a worktree
cards.claim: Only the implement step needs a git worktree; research and planning can run on main.
cards.evidence_detail: Aside; no rationale beyond practice.
cards.landing: Phase routine: worktree use limited to implementation phases

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I threw that research out and kicked off a new one
cards.claim: Read the research output yourself, discard it when wrong, and rerun with more steering; do not build a plan on bad research.
cards.evidence_detail: BAML bug: first research wrongly called the bug invalid.
cards.landing: Refute-by-default reviewers on research/diagnosis outputs; knowledge-store verified diagnoses

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the one built with research fixed the problem in the best place
cards.claim: Two plans for the same bug, one with research and one without, both worked, but only the research-backed one put the fix in the right place and matched codebase test conventions.
cards.evidence_detail: Single paired example; research-backed PR approved by maintainer, other closed.
cards.landing: Justifies a research step before planning in the phase routine

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: ran both plans in parallel and submitted both as PRs
cards.claim: Run competing plans in parallel and keep the one that survives review.
cards.evidence_detail: BAML bug example, one winner out of two PRs.
cards.landing: Workflow-tool orchestration: parallel-plan then judge pattern

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: 7 hours (3 hours on research/plans, 4 hours on implementation) and shipped 35k LOC
cards.claim: A 7-hour paired session split 3h research/plans and 4h implementation produced about 35k LOC (cancellation and WASM) estimated at 3-5 senior-engineer days each.
cards.evidence_detail: 35k LOC, 7 h, estimate by Vaibhav of 3-5 days per PR; one PR merged, one still open at the time.
cards.landing: Time split benchmark for phase effort (roughly 40% front-loaded)

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: You have to engage with your task when you're doing this or it WILL NOT WORK.
cards.claim: The method requires continuous human engagement; there is no magic prompt, and human review at the high-leverage points is what makes it work on hard problems.
cards.evidence_detail: Argued from the BAML and parquet-java sessions.
cards.landing: Owner-view and review gates in the phase routine

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the research steps didn't go deep enough through the dependency tree
cards.claim: A failure case: parquet-java hadoop removal failed in 7 hours because research did not go deep enough and nobody involved was a codebase expert.
cards.evidence_detail: One failed 7-hour session; lesson is that an expert in the codebase is needed.
cards.landing: Research depth check (transitive dependencies) and owner/expert review of research before planning

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a bad line of a plan could lead to hundreds of bad lines of code.
cards.claim: Review leverage rises as you move upstream: a bad line of research yields thousands of bad code lines, a bad plan line hundreds, so review research and plans before code.
cards.evidence_detail: Orders-of-magnitude illustration, no measurement.
cards.landing: Reviewer scope: plan and diagnosis reviews ahead of PR-diff review (Opus reviewer per PR)

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I can't read 2000 lines of golang daily. But I can read 200 lines
cards.claim: Humans cannot keep up with reading AI-generated code but can read a 200-line implementation plan, so plans and research become the shared artifacts for team understanding.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal experience with 2000-line PRs every few days.
cards.landing: One-page owner view; plan-sized review artifacts

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the most important part of code review is mental alignment
cards.claim: Code review's main job is mental alignment; with high AI output, much of the codebase becomes unfamiliar to every engineer, so the process must keep people on the same page and help them learn unfamiliar areas quickly.
cards.evidence_detail: Adopts Blake Smith's framing; supported by team experience.
cards.landing: Owner view and closing message content; research docs as onboarding for the owner

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I still read the tests pretty carefully
cards.claim: When he stopped reading every PR line, he still read tests carefully and treated specs as the source of truth.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal practice after an 8-week transition.
cards.landing: Reviewer focus on tests (fail-before/pass-after) over implementation lines

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: our team of three is averaging about $12k on opus per month
cards.claim: Reported spend: a three-person team averages about $12k per month on Opus.
cards.evidence_detail: Single stated figure, about $4k per person per month; no breakdown.
cards.landing: Cost baseline for effort routing and verifier spend

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Our intern shipped 2 PRs on his first day, and 10 on his 8th day.
cards.claim: Onboarding claim: with the workflow an intern shipped 2 PRs on day one and 10 on day eight.
cards.evidence_detail: Two numbers, one person; also: 8-week team transition, 6 PRs in a day, a 2-week race-condition failure.
cards.landing: Cold-resume trial framing: a newcomer (or fresh agent) productive from repo artifacts

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the specs became our source of truth for what was being built and why
cards.claim: Adopt spec-driven development: commit the specs and prompts, not just final code, since discarding them is like checking in a binary and throwing away the source.
cards.evidence_detail: Credits Sean Grove; his team's 8-week transition.
cards.landing: Decisions journal and plan files kept in repo as the source of truth

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I won't even try to convince you that research/plan/implement is the right approach
cards.claim: Research/plan/implement is not claimed to suit most teams; the requirement is any process that keeps people aligned and lets them learn unfamiliar code fast.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated caveat.
cards.landing: Treat the phase routine as one instance of an alignment process, judged on that goal

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Subagents are not about playing house and anthropomorphizing roles.
cards.claim: Against role-playing agent personas: split work by context need, not by job title.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated with link to an X post.
cards.landing: Guidance for designing custom agents and reviewer roles

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: how the "thoughts tool" works
cards.claim: HumanLayer shares and manages the research/plan markdown files through a 'thoughts' tool (shared thoughts directory), left unexplained here.
cards.evidence_detail: Pointer only; the example repo paths show thoughts/shared/research and thoughts/shared/plans.
cards.landing: A durable research/plans directory in the repo (knowledge-store neighbour)

cards.source_title: Getting AI to Work in Complex Codebases
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: AI tools often lead to a lot of rework
cards.claim: Cites the Stanford study of 100k developers: much AI-shipped code reworks last week's slop, and AI is often counter-productive on brownfield and complex tasks.
cards.evidence_detail: Secondhand: commits of 100k developers analysed by Yegor's team; no figures in text (charts as images).
cards.landing: Motivation for rework/slop tracking; FixFlow is brownfield

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: no amount of harness engineering or loopsmaxxing can solve what is fundamentally a model-training issue.
cards.claim: Harness engineering and loops cannot fix models' inability to maintain codebase quality, because that is a training (RL reward) problem.
cards.evidence_detail: Argued from how RLVR rewards work and from his own lights-off experience; he says he cannot prove it.
cards.landing: Limits of the verifier/harness layer; keep human review in the loop

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: there is no penalty for eroding codebase maintainability
cards.claim: Coding RL rewards (FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS tests) never penalise design erosion, which explains try/catch-everywhere and lazy type casts.
cards.evidence_detail: Worked example from SWE-bench Multilingual fastlane task; no measurement of slop rates.
cards.landing: Reviewer checklist for design smells the model is not trained against (blanket try/catch, casts); mypy-strict and lint-imports already backstop some

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Throw away any edits it made to the test files
cards.claim: Benchmark graders discard the agent's test-file edits before applying the held-out test patch because models were caught commenting out or mocking failing tests.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes grading procedure and says models were caught gaming tests.
cards.landing: Verifier design: judge from a clean checkout with the tests the agent could not edit; reviewer asks for fail-before/pass-after on tests the author did not alter

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Tests give you feedback in seconds, but the cost function of bad architecture is measured in weeks
cards.claim: Quality verification is far harder than pass/fail because bad-design cost shows up weeks or months later and cannot be backpropagated to the decision.
cards.evidence_detail: Conceptual argument with diagram.
cards.landing: Why verifiers cannot be fully automated; add lagging indicators (rework, incident links) to the review loop

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: They don't move the ceiling, because the ceiling is whatever we managed to teach the model
cards.claim: More review agents and tokens raise the floor by catching dumb mistakes but do not raise the quality ceiling; a model judging quality is bounded by its training.
cards.evidence_detail: Reasoning argument; no data in this essay.
cards.landing: Cap verifier spend and layers; stacking refuters has diminishing returns beyond catching basic defects

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if a model could reliably tell good code from bad, it might have written the good version
cards.claim: Model-as-judge for maintainability is circular: a reliable judge would imply a reliable author.
cards.evidence_detail: Argument; Frontier Code's judge-over-diff cited as only a start.
cards.landing: Skepticism toward LLM judge panels for design quality; keep deterministic checks (import-linter, alembic check, mutation-style fail-before)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it penalizes the model for writing tests that don't fail on the pre-patch code
cards.claim: Frontier Code's deterministic quality check: penalise tests that do not fail on pre-patch code (mutation-testing flavour), plus a judge model over the diff against quality rules.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes Cognition's benchmark design; no results.
cards.landing: Matches 'fail-before/pass-after per register id' reviewer rule; could be made a mechanical check

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we went full lights-off. Just read the specs and the tickets
cards.claim: HumanLayer's own lights-off trial (July 2025) ended with an unsolvable bug, site downtime and a two-week manual rewrite of patterns by the cofounder around the third incident in November.
cards.evidence_detail: First-person account; about two weeks digging through output, then two weeks rewrite; no metrics.
cards.landing: Rationale for keeping human code review; a lights-off phase should be treated as a risk

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: THERE ARE NO GOOD BENCHMARKS for a model's ability to maintain codebase quality
cards.claim: Models improved at one-off problems but not clearly at keeping codebase quality over time, and no good benchmark exists to show otherwise.
cards.evidence_detail: Explicitly unprovable; model-generation sketch chart only.
cards.landing: Do not assume newer models relax review; measure on own repo

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: an agent-built codebase starts to struggle after maybe three to six months
cards.claim: Agent-built codebases start to slow and need a different approach to adding features after roughly three to six months, making 'brownfield' arrive much sooner.
cards.evidence_detail: Impression, no data.
cards.landing: Plan for codebase-health work; FixFlow is already in this regime

cards.author: other
cards.quote: +25% more review comments, +22.7% longer comments, +31.3% of PRs skip review entirely
cards.claim: Dex cites the Faros AI report (as image alt text): since AI tools spread, review quality fell, 31.3% of PRs skip review, incidents per PR up 242.7%, bugs per developer up 54%; he calls it correlation, not a smoking gun.
cards.evidence_detail: Faros figures: +25% comments, +22.7% longer, +31.3% skipped review, +242.7% incidents per PR, +57.9% monthly incidents, +54% bugs per developer; Dex flags it as correlational.
cards.landing: Evidence for not letting PRs merge unreviewed; context for the Opus reviewer per PR

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Is a skill issue -- that if you're not getting good results
cards.claim: Against the 'skill issue / spend more tokens / stop reading code' advice: he argues the limits are model-training limits, not user error.
cards.evidence_detail: Rhetorical position.
cards.landing: Resist a token-maxxing posture for verifiers (links to L1 effort routing)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Review still takes hours or days.
cards.claim: When agents build in minutes, human review becomes the bottleneck; adding agentic review and regression testing helps but review remains the constraint.
cards.evidence_detail: Diagram-driven argument.
cards.landing: Budget the owner's review time as the scarce resource; owner one-page view

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: less time reviewing every line
cards.claim: Front-load alignment: about 1 hour of up-front planning cuts rework and review from roughly 6 hours to 20 minutes (figure caption).
cards.evidence_detail: Illustrative numbers in a diagram alt text, not measured.
cards.landing: Justification for the plan-first phase routine; plan review before code

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a short doc that pins down *what* we're building and *why*
cards.claim: Product review: a short doc fixing the user problem and what success looks like (a readable post-ship signal), kept in product terms; technical thoughts are jotted for later phases.
cards.evidence_detail: Team practice with screenshots; not for copy tweaks, one-off scripts or bugs with obvious repro.
cards.landing: A product-review skill or plan-template section (problem, success signal) for owner-facing phases

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: A rough HTML mockup of the actual screen settles an argument
cards.claim: Mock up UI as rough HTML instead of describing it; a mockup settles arguments that paragraphs prolong.
cards.evidence_detail: Screenshots of product-review docs with JSON workflow outline and two mockups.
cards.landing: Skill for owner-facing UI phases (web manager screens)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we do author-opt-in reviews
cards.claim: Author-opt-in review: the author picks the eventual PR reviewer and walks through product/tech specs with them before coding, asynchronously via doc comments or live.
cards.evidence_detail: Team practice.
cards.landing: Owner pre-code review of the plan PR (draft PR with 'Plan @ sha') is this practice

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: how the services, endpoints, schemas, queues, and stores talk to each other
cards.claim: System architecture step: sequence diagrams, contract/endpoint shapes and data models/query shapes, with the warning that Mermaid can give a false sense of alignment.
cards.evidence_detail: Template with examples; says architecture alone is insufficient for quality.
cards.landing: Plan template sections for new slices (contract, schema, sequence)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: criminally underemphasized in agentic coding: **program design**
cards.claim: Program design: before implementation, agree types, method signatures, program layout and call stacks, drafted by the model and argued by the human, so decisions are made before review.
cards.evidence_detail: His first skill version was 'hard to read, exhausting'; pseudocode visualisations won over Mermaid.
cards.landing: A program-design skill in .claude/skills/ (types/signatures/call-tree/file-tree diff per plan)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: **Call-stack trees**, for any orchestration or control-flow change.
cards.claim: Use diff-syntax call-stack trees and file-tree diffs (NEW/MODIFIED) in plans so reviewers see control flow and layout changes; endorses call graphs in planning (Dillon Mulroy).
cards.evidence_detail: Example snippets; no results.
cards.landing: Plan template; the harness review skipped call-graph tooling, but this is a lightweight text version (marks a re-open of that skip)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: every one of them is a decision you'd otherwise be making implicitly during code review
cards.claim: Types, signatures and call trees are cheap to produce and surface decisions that would otherwise be made at the most expensive moment, in code review.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated.
cards.landing: Plan-phase gate: signatures and layout agreed before code

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Models love what I call "horizontal plans"
cards.claim: Models plan in stack order (migrations, service, API, frontend) so nothing can be touched until the end; prefer vertical slices (tracer bullets) starting in the middle with mock data and curl/browser checks at each step.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's own pre-AI habit: contract and mock first, frontend, wire services, migrations, business logic, error handling.
cards.landing: Ship-plan phase shape: each phase a touchable slice; plan template rejects stack-ordered plans

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Checking 100-200 lines and resteering is a lot cheaper
cards.claim: Review code at each slice (100-200 lines) when quality matters, and send the agent off on only 1-3 slices at a time rather than reviewing 2k+ lines at once.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal practice; sizes stated.
cards.landing: Slice/PR size cap and per-slice review in the phase routine

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: ~40% of tasks get oneshot or oneshot w/ 1-2 rounds of light feedback
cards.claim: Task-size routing: about 40% of tasks are oneshot; medium tasks get product/system design in one plan doc with no phases; large tasks get all steps (product skipped for refactors).
cards.evidence_detail: His guess ('I would guess the distribution is roughly').
cards.landing: A triage rule at phase start so small phases skip the full routine; route effort by size

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: You don't have too many PRs. You have too many bad PRs.
cards.claim: PRs needing 20% rework (AI oneshot PRs closer to 50%) burden submitter and reviewer; a good PR is quick to review.
cards.evidence_detail: 20% and 50% are his estimates ('that's generous').
cards.landing: Reviewer outcome metric: rework rate per PR; gate on PR quality not count

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: move 2-3x faster, safely
cards.claim: Closing stance: accept the constraints, aim for 2-3x not 10-100x, learn model constraints by use, seek leverage, and read the code.
cards.evidence_detail: Advice list: learn constraints, optimise within them, seek leverage, read the dang code.
cards.landing: Expectation setting for ship plan velocity

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a bunch of potentially-bad model tics that you can head off during this phase
cards.claim: Architecture review is high leverage because it catches known model tics early, but alone it does not give high-quality code.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated.
cards.landing: Known-tics list in a skill or reviewer prompt (model failure modes for this repo)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: building blocks for your software factory" and "better verifiers for software maintainability
cards.claim: HumanLayer's direction is toward building blocks for a factory and better maintainability verifiers.
cards.evidence_detail: Product pitch (PS section).
cards.landing: Signals what verifiers are missing; no actionable config

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: only 25-50% of the time to ship a feature was writing the code itself
cards.claim: Pre-AI, coding was only 25-50% of feature time (e.g. 2-4 hours of a two-day feature); AI that only writes code leaves the rest unaccelerated.
cards.evidence_detail: Illustrative wheel diagrams; coding 2-4 h down to 10-20 min.
cards.landing: Measure where phase time goes (plan/review/test), not only coding time
cards.inventory_ref: Essay side quest (repo line 22, wsff line 110)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you use AI to help you plan and align, then you actually get closer to 2-3x faster.
cards.claim: Using AI for planning and alignment, not just code, shrinks review and testing time too, giving roughly 2-3x.
cards.evidence_detail: Diagram reasoning.
cards.landing: Plan-phase AI assistance and aligned plan as the lever
cards.inventory_ref: Essay side quest (repo line 22, wsff line 110)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: about 80% of the expected pain is gone in the first few minutes
cards.claim: 80/20 rule: expected pain (P(rework) x cost) falls on an inverse-exponential curve; yolo prompt ~50% rework (2 min), afternoon hand-spec ~10% (5 h), all by hand ~0% (20 h); don't spend 6 hours where 10 minutes removes 80%.
cards.evidence_detail: Three illustrative points (50%/10%/0% at 2 min/5 h/20 h), explicitly assumed, not measured.
cards.landing: Effort routing for planning depth: cap plan time per phase; short plans first
cards.inventory_ref: Essay side quest (repo line 22, wsff line 110)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you build a harness but you don't own the weights
cards.claim: Claude Code won partly because Anthropic RL'd the model inside its harness; tool shape matters (SWE-Agent), so harness tools should match what the model was trained on.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites SWE-Agent 2024 and OpenAI's talk; no numbers.
cards.landing: Prefer the built-in tools and standard tool shapes over custom ones; keep custom agents/tools few and simple

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Those people are all really dang smart
cards.claim: Counter-claim to StrongDM-style lights-off factories and OpenAI Symphony: he found no definitive outcome data from StrongDM and lists outages from agent mishaps.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites FT outages, Mario's talk, Matt Pocock; no figures of his own.
cards.landing: Keep human gate on merges; treat factory claims as unproven

gaps: Images, charts and slide figures in all four sources were not viewed; the Faros figures are taken from image alt text only.

The blog post (2025-08-29) is textually identical to ace-fca.md at its earlier version, so it was not carded separately; any differences from the later 2025-10/12 edits to ace-fca.md could not be diffed because only the current repo version and the blog were provided.
